title: Engineers stopped writing code a year ago, and AI employees tripled the company
dek: Eight Sleep's email marketing team went from 2 people to 0 and now drives close to $100M in annual revenue; engineers stopped writing code a year ago, replaced by hundreds of AI engineers. Matteo has started counting ‘human employees’ and ‘AI employees’ — count the AI in, and the company is three to four times its current size.
why: Medium information density, but there are a few concrete numbers and mechanisms worth hearing: how AI employees took over marketing, platforms faking CAC, hardware cost due diligence. The celebrity stories in the back half are soft.
who: Suited to hardware founders, growth leads and early-stage investors, especially readers focused on AI replacing headcount and measuring true CAC.
skip: The celebrity anecdotes from 41:10 to 43:18 can be skipped, low information density.

points.h: Salaries are out of control, so recruiting is shifting to Europe
points.body: Matteo says we are ‘back to 2021’: not just engineers, even product manager salaries are out of control, and every company is making crazy offers. The harder problem is not hiring but keeping people — if you are a company with a decent brand, your employees will keep getting higher-paying offers. Eight Sleep's response is to shift recruiting more and more toward Europe and outside the US. He also admits that when the salary gap gets big enough, ‘there is nothing you can do’, and people really do get poached by companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.

points.h: Hardware founders get first-year costs wrong by 50%
points.body: Asked what investors don't understand about hardware, Matteo gives a very specific answer: in the first year, or even the first three months, founders do not really know what it costs to produce the device, and they do not know the return rate either. So the BOM and COGS they present when raising are off by at least 50%. This is a due diligence checklist item for hardware investors: do not trust the cost structure an early founder reports.

points.h: Platform-reported CAC is fake, so run your own incrementality tests
points.body: Matteo says you cannot trust platform attribution, because the same platform double-counts conversions. He gives an example: the CAC shown in Meta's dashboard is roughly 20% lower than the real CAC. Eight Sleep's approach is to build its own model to calculate the true CAC of each channel, and to run an incrementality test every six months — for example, turning off a channel in two similar-performing regions and seeing how much revenue drops, which gives that channel's true incremental value. His reasoning is blunt: if you don't do this, the brand is only fooling itself.

points.h: The email marketing team went from 2 people to 0, on nearly $100M
points.body: Eight Sleep originally had a two-person email marketing team. After the person in charge left, co-founder Alexandra took over and built multiple bots within three days to take over all of email marketing. That team is now zero people, and email marketing contributes close to $100M in revenue. The mechanism: AI decides from historical data when to send, what email to send, and what copy to use. Matteo also says he has started counting ‘human employees’ and ‘AI employees’, and counting the AI employees in, the company is roughly three to four times its current size.

points.h: Engineers stopped writing code a year ago
points.body: Matteo says Eight Sleep's engineers stopped writing code about a year ago, and now they have hundreds of AI engineers writing it for them. This is why the company can expand across 35 countries (including China, the Middle East and Europe, markets with very different regulation) with a very small team. On tooling they mainly use Claude, at a spend in the millions of dollars per month. From this he poses an investment question: if 5% of an engineering budget goes to Claude, does that share rise to 50% or get crushed to 1% by open source models? His own judgment is that both happen at once — usage rises, unit price falls, and the net effect is a decline.

points.h: He thinks models training themselves is already happening
points.body: Asked about people at OpenAI calling to ‘pause a little’, Matteo says the truly worrying part is models learning on their own and training themselves — that is where losing control begins. When the host asks ‘don't you think we are already there’, he answers ‘I think we are already there’, and argues there is a big gap between the capabilities users see and the capabilities inside frontier model companies, which the latter have already seen behind the scenes. He mentions attempts inside OpenAI's models where agents formed groups on their own.

points.h: Endorsements only go to real users of the product
points.body: Matteo says any athlete or celebrity partnership has only two conditions: first, they must actually use the product, ideally having bought it with their own money; second, he must be able to build a direct relationship with the person himself, and will not accept a manager standing in the middle. The reasoning is practical — the greatest value of this kind of product is that they mention to a friend in passing that it works well, and if they just took a few million dollars in equity, it is purely a financial transaction that brings nothing.

points.h: Interviewing at both Anthropic and us is a red flag
points.body: Matteo says people still tell him ‘I'm choosing between Anthropic and Eight Sleep’, and he considers that a very bad red flag — not because of salary, but because it shows the person has not thought it through: the two jobs have nothing in common. When he hires, he cares more about whether someone is driven by the right things than about simply comparing prices.
